findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the supersedes proof identify the store even when the local epoch is absent (for example, carry the pre-rewrite root commit SHA(s) in the superseding record and require the local HEAD's root to match), and add a test where an unrelated pre-epoch store against a [null]-lineage remote still refuses with DIVERGED.
evidence: Plan: "whose new `epoch_lineage` list names the local epoch (JSON `null` stands for the pre-epoch/absent record). That lineage is the proof that the remote is a rewrite of THIS store, not an unrelated store"
compat.store_epoch_problem: 'An absent record and a present record with no epoch both describe the pre-reclaim store' — absent is shared by every legacy store
sync.py:111-112: 'Refuse one with ticket events: independently built histories need operator recovery, not implicit grafting.'
Testing covers only 'different epoch, lineage not naming the local epoch', not an unrelated pre-epoch store against a [null]-lineage remote
findings.finding: The lineage proof does not identify the store when the local epoch is absent. 'JSON null stands for the pre-epoch/absent record' means that the first reclaim of ANY store stamps lineage [null]. Every store today is pre-epoch, because nothing stamps an epoch yet. So any unrelated pre-epoch store whose remote has been reclaimed once satisfies 'lineage names the local epoch' and is force-reset. That is the exact 'independently built histories need operator recovery' case that the current refusal (sync.py:111-121) protects. All of that store's events would count as 'unpushed', the oldest would usually be past the horizon, and the whole local store would be thrown away except for a local backup ref.
scenarios: An operator points an independently initialized store (absent epoch, real tickets) at a remote that has been reclaimed once (lineage [null]). Today it refuses with DIVERGED. Under the plan it is silently reset and its events dropped as 'stale'.
findings.suggested_fix: Have superseding_record also record the superseded history's root commit(s) (e.g. a `superseded_roots` list from `git rev-list --max-parents=0` on the pre-rewrite tip). remote_epoch_supersedes_local then requires lineage ∋ local epoch AND local HEAD's root ∈ superseded_roots. Malformed or missing roots fail closed to the existing DIVERGED refusal.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the supersedes proof store-specific when the local epoch is null, and add a test that an unrelated remote with lineage [null] still refuses with DIVERGED.
evidence: "JSON `null` stands for the pre-epoch/absent record"
"That lineage is the proof that the remote is a rewrite of THIS store, not an unrelated store, so unrelated stores keep today's refusal."
Testing covers only an unrelated remote whose 'lineage [does] not nam[e] the local epoch', never the case of a local null epoch against an unrelated remote whose lineage also contains null.
findings.finding: Using JSON null as a lineage entry for the pre-epoch record does not identify a store. Every pre-epoch store has the same 'null' local epoch, so a remote whose lineage contains null 'supersedes' ANY pre-epoch clone. An unrelated store's first reclaimed baseline would therefore be accepted as a rewrite of this store, and the clone would be hard-reset onto foreign data. This contradicts the plan's stated purpose of the lineage: the proof that the remote is a rewrite of THIS store, not an unrelated store.
findings.location: Approach — 'whose new `epoch_lineage` list names the local epoch (JSON `null` stands for the pre-epoch/absent record)'; Testing — Failure/edge bullet
scenarios: A pre-epoch clone of store A reconnects to a remote that was swapped to store B's first reclaimed baseline (lineage [null]). The supersedes predicate returns true, the clone is reset onto B, and its events are replayed onto or discarded against the wrong store.
findings.suggested_fix: For a null local epoch, require additional proof before overriding. One option is that the remote record carries the pre-swap tip commit (or a store id) that must be an ancestor of, or equal to, a commit reachable from local HEAD. Otherwise keep the DIVERGED refusal. Alternatively, have superseding_record stamp a minted id in place of null. Add a test for an unrelated remote with lineage [null] against a pre-epoch clone.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Realign the stale classification to the parent's 'last remote convergence older than N days' definition (e.g. using the newest local commit reachable from the last-fetched remote-tracking ref / merge-base date), or record in the parent/ADR that the oldest-unpushed-event age is the accepted proxy and add a test for a long-disconnected clone that wrote only recently.
evidence: Parent C3: 'any clone whose last remote convergence is older than N days is forced to reset local `tickets` to remote on reconnect and may NOT reintroduce E by merge/rebase'.
ADR 0106 §5: 'A clone whose **last convergence predates the horizon** ("stale") ... MUST override local with remote'.
Leaf step 2 bases the classification on unpushed-event age, and its Testing section only builds clones whose unpushed event age matches how long they were disconnected.
findings.finding: The leaf redefines the parent's stale criterion. Parent C3 defines stale as 'a clone whose last remote convergence is older than N days', and ADR §5 says such a clone must override rather than reintroduce local history. The leaf instead calls a clone stale iff 'its oldest unpushed event's `ts` is older than now − horizon'. An unpushed event written at time t only shows that the last convergence happened before t. So that age is a lower bound on how long ago the clone last converged, not an upper bound. A clone that was disconnected for more than N days but only wrote recently is classified fresh and replays its events. The parent requires that clone to be force-reset with accepted loss.
findings.location: Approach step 2 ('Stale vs fresh ... Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence')
scenarios: A clone fetches and pushes nothing for 45 days, writes one event on day 44, then reconnects. The leaf classifies it fresh and replays the event, while the parent's rule classifies it stale and requires a forced reset.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an AC that after the override `write_blocking_divergence` returns no block, and that for a fresh clone a subsequent push leaves the throwaway remote tip equal to the replay commit.
evidence: Context: "Such a clone stays wedged forever, its writes are refused by freshness.write_blocking_divergence"
AC: "replayed in one commit on top of the remote"
findings.finding: The ACs stop short of the end state the Context promises. The problem is that the clone 'stays wedged forever, its writes are refused'. The fresh AC checks only that a local replay commit exists, while the plan says 'the normal push path then delivers' it. No AC asserts that after the override `freshness.write_blocking_divergence` no longer blocks writes, or that the replay commit actually reaches the remote.
scenarios: The override succeeds, but stale divergence state or an un-triggered push leaves the clone still refusing writes.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an AC/test that after the override a new ticket write succeeds (write_blocking_divergence returns no block) and, for a fresh clone, the replay commit reaches the throwaway remote.
evidence: "its writes are refused by `freshness.write_blocking_divergence`"
AC1/AC2 only check "HEAD equals the remote commit" and "replayed in one commit on top of the remote"; "which the normal push path then delivers" is untested.
findings.finding: The stated problem is that a wedged clone's 'writes are refused by `freshness.write_blocking_divergence`'. No acceptance criterion or test shows that end state is fixed after an override, meaning that a subsequent write is accepted and the divergence state clears. There is also no test that the replayed commit is actually pushed. The ACs prove repository shape (the HEAD and parent relationships) but not the user-observable un-wedging.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that the supersedes check runs before the `_carries_ticket_events` split, so an empty store facing a superseding remote also takes the override (a plain reset), and add a test for that case.
evidence: sync.py:113-123: the `_carries_ticket_events` check splits into a refusal and `_union_merge(... --allow-unrelated-histories)`
sync.py:145-148: _union_merge refuses when store_epoch_merge_target reports a problem
compat.store_epoch_problem: absent vs a stamped epoch is a mismatch, so it refuses
findings.finding: The plan doesn't say where the supersedes check goes relative to the existing empty-store branch. In _do_reconverge, an unrelated local store with no ticket events goes to `_union_merge(..., '--allow-unrelated-histories')`. That calls store_epoch_merge_target, which refuses any epoch mismatch. If the override is only wired where the plan points ('call the override when the remote supersedes; otherwise keep the existing refusal'), an empty pre-epoch store facing a superseding remote is refused by the epoch guard and never joins. The 'no unpushed events' test uses a non-empty clone, so it would not catch this.
scenarios: A freshly initialized empty store (compat record with no epoch) syncs against a reclaimed remote and gets an epoch-guard refusal on every tick.
findings.suggested_fix: In _do_reconverge's no-merge-base branch: pin the remote commit first. If remote_epoch_supersedes_local(tracker, pinned), run stale_override with that pinned commit and return. Otherwise keep the existing _carries_ticket_events refusal and union-merge logic unchanged.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Either get the epoch-lineage stamping obligation recorded in the parent/ADR and in S2's Scope+ACs (S2 must stamp `superseding_record` onto the swapped baseline) before landing this leaf, or realign the leaf's detection to the parent's merge-base rule.
evidence: Leaf: 'when HEAD and the remote share no merge-base and the remote epoch supersedes the local one' → override; otherwise 'keep the existing refusal unchanged'.

ADR 0106 §5 (parent's adopted contract): 'This is detected by comparing the clone's `tickets` merge-base against the checkpoint: no common ancestor within the retained graph ⇒ stale ⇒ forced override.'
Parent C3: 'any clone whose last remote convergence is older than N days is **forced to reset local `tickets` to remote** on reconnect'.
S2 (4b2a) Scope/ACs cover the --force-with-lease CAS, S3 bundle-set replacement, backup ref and rollback re-convergence. Epoch or lineage stamping is never mentioned.
S1 (bdf3, closed): search_files 'epoch' in src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_collapse.py finds only a `_raw_date(epoch_seconds…)` helper and no store-epoch stamping.
findings.finding: The leaf changes the parent's C3 detection rule. Parent/ADR 0106 §5 says 'no common ancestor within the retained graph ⇒ stale ⇒ forced override'. The leaf only overrides when there is no merge-base AND the remote's .store-compat.json carries a superseding `epoch` whose `epoch_lineage` names the local epoch. No sibling ticket is assigned to write that record. S1 (bdf3) is closed and its engine stamps no epoch. S2 (4b2a) has nothing about epochs in its Scope or ACs. So the leaf delivers a `superseding_record` helper 'that S2's publish-swap will use' and puts an obligation on a sibling that neither the parent nor that sibling contains. If nothing stamps the record, every rewritten remote produces the existing DIVERGED refusal, and the parent's enforced-override goal (C3) does not hold.
findings.location: Approach ¶1 ('A reclaimed baseline is identified by a remote record whose `epoch` differs ... AND whose new `epoch_lineage` list names the local epoch') and the `superseding_record` paragraph ('that S2's publish-swap will use'); parent 536b C3 / ADR 0106 §5 detection clause
scenarios: S2 lands as currently specified: the rewritten remote keeps the old .store-compat.json epoch, `remote_epoch_supersedes_local` is false, and every clone stays wedged in DIVERGED (the exact problem the leaf's Context sets out to fix).
The S3 dry-run harness exercises the override against an S1-produced baseline, which has no epoch record, and the override never fires.
findings.suggested_fix: Following the parent-wins rule: add a comment or edit on epic 536b (and an amendment to ADR 0106 §5) saying that a rewritten baseline must carry a superseding `.store-compat.json` epoch whose `epoch_lineage` names the prior epoch, and that this lineage is the C3 detection proof. Add an AC to S2 (4b2a) that each publish adapter stamps `compat.superseding_record(...)` into the baseline tree before the swap. Then re-review this leaf against the updated parent.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State how the epoch-lineage predicate handles a rollback to the pre-reclaim backup ref (old epoch) so S2's rollback re-convergence, which relies on this override, can work, and add a fixture or AC for it or record in the parent that S2 must restore a re-stamped successor epoch.
evidence: Parent Risk/rollback: 'immutable backup ref `refs/tickets-backup/pre-reclaim-<date>` ... the swap is one revertible step'.
S2 (depends_on aff9) AC: 'a client on the rewritten baseline is force-overridden back onto the restored ref'; Scope: 'force-override per the C3 stale-clone protocol'.
Leaf: override only when the remote record's `epoch_lineage` 'names the local epoch'; otherwise 'keep the existing refusal unchanged'.
The leaf has no test or AC for a remote rolled back to an earlier epoch.
findings.finding: The leaf's lineage rule only works in one direction, which conflicts with the parent's rollback clause. The parent says 'the swap is one revertible step, revertible to the backup ref'. Sibling S2 must force-override clients that already reconciled onto the rewritten baseline back onto the restored ref 'per the C3 stale-clone protocol', and S2 depends on this leaf. A restored pre-reclaim ref carries the OLD epoch, and its lineage cannot name the NEW epoch the client now has. Under the leaf's predicate that remote does not supersede the local one, so the leaf keeps the DIVERGED refusal and the rollback re-convergence path is blocked. The only way around it is to restore something other than the backup ref (a re-stamped copy), which contradicts the parent's 'immutable backup ref' rollback.
findings.location: Approach ('remote_epoch_supersedes_local' predicate; 'unrelated stores keep today's refusal'); Acceptance Criteria #3; parent 536b 'Risk / rollback' clause and S2 rollback re-convergence AC
scenarios: A swap is published, some clones reconcile onto epoch E1 (lineage [null]), operators roll back to the backup ref (epoch null), and those clones get DIVERGED forever instead of being force-overridden.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the default that stale_override takes an injectable `now` (or fixtures write back-dated `{ts}` filenames), and add tests for the mixed stale+fresh discard, the exact-horizon boundary, and a two-hop `epoch_lineage`.
evidence: "a clone whose only unpushed event is older than the horizon" — the mechanism for making it old is unstated.
Approach: "stale iff its oldest unpushed event's ts is older than now − [reclaim].horizon_days"
findings.finding: The test plan does not say how 'now' versus event `ts` is controlled. The plan does not state whether the clock is injected or event filenames are fabricated with back-dated `ts`. Three cases are also missing. The first is the mixed case: one unpushed event older than the horizon plus recent ones, which by the rule discards all of them, including the recent writes. The second is the boundary at exactly the horizon. The third is a multi-hop lineage (the remote swapped twice while the clone was offline).
scenarios: The executor hardcodes a wall-clock-dependent fixture that flakes.
Discarding fresh writes in the mixed case is never confirmed as intended behaviour.
findings.suggested_fix: Give the override entry point a `now: datetime | None = None` parameter. Fixtures write event files named with ts = now − (horizon_days + 1) days for stale cases and now − 1 day for fresh cases.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add `docs/adr/0106-remote-anchored-history-reclamation.md` §5 to Scope, or state why it stays unchanged, so the ADR records the lineage proof, the horizon-based stale/fresh split, and fresh-clone replay.
evidence: docs/adr/0106-remote-anchored-history-reclamation.md:119-121: 'This is detected by comparing the clone's `tickets` merge-base against the checkpoint: no common ancestor within the retained graph ⇒ stale ⇒ forced override.'
Plan Approach steps 2 and 4 add a horizon-based stale/fresh split and replay of fresh clones
Scope's docs entry is only `docs/concurrency.md`
findings.finding: ADR 0106 §5 is the governing ADR. It says the stale case is detected by merge-base alone ('no common ancestor within the retained graph ⇒ stale ⇒ forced override') and does not mention replaying fresh clones. The plan changes this contract: it requires an epoch-lineage proof, classifies stale vs fresh by the horizon, and replays fresh clones' unpushed events. Yet ADR 0106 is not in Scope, so the ADR and the implementation would disagree.
scenarios: A later reader of ADR 0106 expects every unrelated-history clone to be overridden with nothing kept, but the code replays a fresh clone's events and refuses when there is no lineage proof.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a Scope bullet: 'docs/adr/0106-remote-anchored-history-reclamation.md §5: amend detection to the epoch-lineage proof and record fresh-clone replay vs stale-clone discard.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Decide whether fsck_tracker_health.py's DIVERGED advice and _seam.py's write-refusal text should recognise the superseded-epoch case (e.g. 'sync will override from the remote'), and add them to Scope or say explicitly that they are left unchanged.
evidence: src/rebar/_commands/fsck_tracker_health.py:214-221 DIVERGED message recommends fsck-recover or re-clone
src/rebar/_commands/_seam.py:400-407 write refusal advises fsck / fsck-recover / maintenance
The plan's Context says these writes are 'refused by `freshness.write_blocking_divergence`', but neither file is in Scope
findings.finding: Two operator-facing messages still treat 'no common ancestor' as a dead end that needs manual repair. One is fsck's DIVERGED advice ('run `rebar store fsck-recover`, or re-clone and re-init', fsck_tracker_health.py:214-221). The other is the write refusal (_seam.py:400-407, through freshness.write_blocking_divergence). After this change, the superseded-epoch case recovers automatically on the next reconverge. Neither message is in Scope, so operators would still be told to re-clone or recover by hand for a state the system now fixes itself.
findings.location: Scope — consumers of the no-merge-base verdict
scenarios: A fresh clone after a publish-swap tries a write before any read-triggered reconverge. It is refused and told to run manual recovery, which risks exactly the resurrection the story is meant to prevent.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the override atomic: build the replay commit before moving HEAD, then move HEAD exactly once; add a test that interrupts between the backup-ref and HEAD-move steps.
evidence: "Point refs/rebar/stale-override/<utc-stamp> at the old local HEAD ... then reset --hard to the pinned remote commit."
"A fresh clone re-adds its unpushed event files ... in ONE local commit on top of the remote"
findings.finding: The override is not crash-safe or idempotent. Step 3 resets HEAD to the remote before step 4 creates the replay commit. A crash or kill between the two leaves HEAD on the remote commit. The next reconverge then finds a shared merge-base, so the override branch never re-runs, and the fresh clone's unpushed events silently survive only in the backup ref.
scenarios: Process killed (SIGTERM, laptop sleep, OOM) after the reset but before the replay commit on a fresh clone.
findings.suggested_fix: Compute the replay set and build the replay commit object first. Read blobs from old HEAD, build the tree on top of the remote tree with `git commit-tree -p <remote>`, then create the backup ref. Only then move HEAD once, directly to the replay commit (or to the remote for stale/no-op). A crash at any point leaves either the old HEAD (the override re-runs) or the final state.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Document that the stale proxy is an upper bound on last convergence and justify why misclassifying as 'fresh' is safe (via the step-1 uuid rule); state which horizon_days value applies and how clock skew is handled.
evidence: Context: "a clone whose last convergence predates the N-day reclaim horizon OVERRIDE its local tickets"
Approach: "Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence."
findings.finding: The stale classification does not match the ADR's definition. The ADR's trigger is a clone whose last convergence predates the horizon. The oldest unpushed `ts` is only an UPPER bound on last convergence: a clone offline for 60 days that first wrote yesterday is classified fresh. The plan presents the proxy as equivalent ('bounds the clone's last convergence') without acknowledging the direction of the bound. It also does not address that `ts` comes from the clone's own clock (skew), or whose `horizon_days` value applies when the clone's config differs from the publisher's.
scenarios: A long-offline clone with only recent writes is classified fresh and replays.
A clone with a skewed clock, or a different local horizon_days, is misclassified.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State whether current `write_compat_record` preserves unknown keys; if not, document the required ordering (all clones upgraded before S2's swap) or add a minimum-version gate in the compat record.
evidence: "write_compat_record (compat.py:347) preserves epoch_lineage just as it already preserves epoch" — this applies only to new code.
findings.finding: Coexistence with older rebar versions is unaddressed. Clones running pre-change code will not understand `epoch_lineage`. More importantly, an older `write_compat_record` that rewrites `.store-compat.json` would drop the unknown `epoch_lineage` key and push the stripped record. That erases the lineage proof for every other clone. The plan does not say whether old code preserves unknown keys or how mixed versions are handled before S2's publish-swap.
scenarios: After S2 stamps a superseding record, an un-upgraded clone rewrites the compat record and pushes; upgraded stale clones then see no lineage and stay DIVERGED.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the override crash-safe and idempotent: compute the replay set and build the replay commit on top of the remote BEFORE moving HEAD (or record a pending-replay marker that the next reconverge resumes), use collision-proof backup ref names, and add an interrupted-override test.
evidence: "Point `refs/rebar/stale-override/<utc-stamp>` at the old local HEAD ..., then `reset --hard` to the pinned remote commit."
"A fresh clone re-adds its unpushed event files ... in ONE local commit on top of the remote"
The plan describes no recovery or resume path for an interrupted override.
findings.finding: The override is a multi-step, non-atomic sequence: backup ref, then reset --hard, then a replay commit, then a push. Nothing makes it resumable or idempotent. If the process dies (or the replay commit fails) after the reset but before the replay commit, local HEAD equals the remote. The next reconverge then finds a merge-base, never re-enters the override branch, and the fresh clone's unpushed events stay stranded in refs/rebar/stale-override/* with no replay and no warning. The write lock serializes concurrent writers but does not cover crash or retry.
findings.location: Approach steps 3–4 ('Backup, then override' / 'Fresh clones replay')
scenarios: A crash or SIGKILL between the reset and the replay commit on a fresh clone silently loses events that ADR 0106 §5 says must NOT be lost (the loss is only accepted for stale clones).
Two overrides within the same second produce the same <utc-stamp> ref name and one backup overwrites the other.
findings.suggested_fix: Build the replay tree and commit off-worktree (git read-tree/commit-tree on top of the pinned remote commit), then do one atomic `update-ref` of the tickets branch plus a checkout. Either the old HEAD or the remote+replay commit is then always the branch tip. Make the ref name unique, e.g. a stamp plus a short old-HEAD sha.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Define a retirement path for stale-override backup refs (e.g. prune refs older than horizon_days during reconverge or gc, or document a manual `rebar` cleanup) and state whether epoch_lineage is bounded.

No retire or prune step is mentioned anywhere in Scope, Testing or the ACs.
findings.finding: Backup refs under refs/rebar/stale-override/* are created on every override but never retired, so they accumulate. Each one also pins the entire pre-reclaim history locally, which defeats local reclamation of the space the horizon exists to free. epoch_lineage likewise only ever grows, by one entry per publish-swap. The plan defines no cleanup or expiry for either.

scenarios: A clone that crosses several reclaim cycles keeps N backup refs, each retaining a full pre-collapse history object graph indefinitely.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Replace the '(I5) every write auto-pushes' premise with a verified convergence signal, or explicitly state and test how `sync.push=off`/`async` and failed-push clones are classified before work is discarded.
evidence: Plan: "Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence."
docs/concurrency.md:272: '### I5 — Single locked write path' (describes the lock-guarded append/commit, not push)
src/rebar/_store/push.py:147: `if mode == "off": ... return` (delivery disabled)
docs/concurrency.md:755: '`rebar store import` uses `off` internally for its whole run'
sync.py:261-279: inbound reconverge (fetch + reset/merge) runs on reads independently of whether outbound push succeeds
findings.finding: The rule that decides stale vs fresh depends on the claim that 'every write auto-pushes (I5)', so the oldest unpushed write marks the clone's last convergence. Nothing in the codebase backs this. In docs/concurrency.md, I5 is 'Single locked write path', not auto-push. push.py also supports `sync.push = off` (push disabled, returns at push.py:147) and `async` (a detached child that cannot be observed), and `rebar store import` runs with `off`. A clone can also keep fetching on reads while its pushes fail. So an old unpushed event does not show that the clone stopped converging, and the plan never justifies the bound.
scenarios: A clone with `sync.push=off` writes an event 31 days before the swap but fetches every day. It is labelled stale, and its never-delivered event is silently discarded.
An `async` push keeps failing without any output. The clone looks converged inbound, but the stale rule still drops its work.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that the event `ts` is an HLC prefix (event-schema.md:20-24), not a pure wall-clock time, and either justify its use as an age bound or derive event age from a wall-clock source (e.g. commit date).
evidence: Plan: "The clone is *stale* iff its oldest unpushed event's `ts` is older than `now − [reclaim].horizon_days`"

docs/event-schema.md:20-24: '`${timestamp_ns}` — a single-integer Hybrid Logical Clock prefix ... `max(per-clone cache, the target ticket's witnessed max-prefix, time_ns()) + 1`. It tracks wall-clock ns but never ties or inverts'
findings.finding: The plan compares an event's filename `ts` directly with `now − horizon_days`, as if it were a wall-clock time. Per the I2 contract, the prefix is a Hybrid Logical Clock: `max(per-clone cache, the target ticket's witnessed max-prefix, time_ns()) + 1`. It can run ahead of the event's real write time (for example after seeing a peer whose clock is fast). The plan does not acknowledge or bound this, so the age of the oldest unpushed event is not reliably recoverable from the filename.
scenarios: After a clock-skewed peer advanced the HLC, a genuinely stale clone's event carries an inflated prefix. The clone is classified fresh and replays work the ADR says should be discarded.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Base the stale test on the clone's real last convergence, e.g. the committer date of the remote-tracking tip from before the forced fetch, read from the reflog, or the newest local commit shared with it. Alternatively, state and justify why the plan departs from ADR 0106 §5 and fix the incorrect 'bounds the last convergence' rationale.
evidence: Plan: "Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence."
ADR 0106:116,121: 'A clone whose **last convergence predates the horizon** ("stale") ... a stale clone's un-pushed divergent local work is discarded'
sync.py:263: the forced fetch overwrites refs/remotes/<remote>/<branch>. Before that fetch, that ref (still in its reflog) records the clone's actual last convergence point
findings.finding: The stale/fresh test does not measure what ADR 0106 §5 defines. The ADR says stale means 'last convergence predates the horizon'. The plan classifies by the oldest unpushed event's ts and claims this 'bounds the clone's last convergence', but it doesn't. Take a clone that was disconnected for 60 days and wrote one event yesterday: its oldest unpushed event is one day old, so it is classified fresh and replayed, even though its last convergence is 60 days old. The other way round, one old event stuck behind a failed push makes a recently converged clone 'stale' and throws away its recent work. The rationale in step 2 is therefore wrong, and the plan neither implements the ADR's definition nor says why it departs from it.
scenarios: A laptop is offline for 6 weeks and makes one edit before reconnecting. It is classified fresh, against the ADR.
A clone whose push of one event failed 35 days ago, and which has pulled successfully every day since, is classified stale. Its recent unpushed edits are discarded.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Build the replay commit before moving HEAD (index/commit-tree on top of the pinned remote tree), then make a single `reset --hard` to that commit. If the build fails, leave local HEAD untouched and log a WARNING naming the backup ref, and add a test for that failure path.
evidence: Plan: "Point `refs/rebar/stale-override/<utc-stamp>` at the old local HEAD ... then `reset --hard` to the pinned remote commit." followed by "re-adds its unpushed event files ... in ONE local commit on top of the remote"

sync.py: the existing paths already handle transient faults and watchdog timeouts during git operations (_with_transient_fault_retry, _warn_merge_failed), so a failed git step mid-sequence is a real case
Testing has no case for a failed replay commit
findings.finding: Backup → `reset --hard` → replay commit is not atomic. If the replay commit fails after the reset (disk full, a commit/signing failure, a watchdog timeout, the process dying), the fresh clone's unpushed events are gone from the live tree. They exist only in a local backup ref, and no WARNING names it, because the plan only warns in the stale case. On the next sync HEAD shares history with the remote, so the override never runs again and the replay never resumes.
findings.location: Approach steps 3–4 (Backup, then override / Fresh clones replay)
scenarios: A fresh clone resets to the remote, then the replay commit times out. Its recent edits silently disappear from the store, and nothing tells the user.
findings.suggested_fix: In stale_override: write the backup ref; build a temporary index from <pinned>^{tree} plus the unpushed blobs (taken from the old HEAD); write-tree; commit-tree -p <pinned>; then `reset --hard <replay-commit>`. If any step fails before the reset, return without touching HEAD and log the backup ref.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In Approach §2, justify using the oldest-unpushed-event `ts` as the staleness measure against the established time-since-last-sync signal (e.g. the reflog timestamp of `refs/remotes/<remote>/tickets`, as in Cassandra's gc_grace rule), or switch to that signal or combine the two, and add a test for a clone that synced recently but holds an old unpushed event.
evidence: Plan: "The clone is *stale* iff its oldest unpushed event's `ts` is older than `now − [reclaim].horizon_days` ... Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence."
ADR 0106 §5 (docs/adr/0106-remote-anchored-history-reclamation.md:116-121) defines stale as 'last convergence predates the horizon', not 'oldest unpushed event predates the horizon'.

Retrieved: netdata.cloud Cassandra gc_grace guide — 'Node down longer than gc_grace_seconds. Hints expire before the node returns, so missed deletes are never propagated'; Stack Overflow 69098439 — 'never bring a node back online if it has been down for longer than the shortest gc_grace_seconds' (staleness is measured by time since last sync).
Retrieved: git-scm git-rebase 'Recovering from upstream rebase' — git's own recovery is anchored on the remote-tracking ref history, not on content timestamps.
findings.finding: The plan decides whether a clone is stale using a stand-in measure: 'Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence.' That bound only holds one way. The `ts` of an unpushed event is a timestamp the client writes when it creates the event, and it says nothing about when the clone last fetched from the remote. Established practice for the same no-resurrection problem measures time since the last successful sync: Cassandra's rule that a node down longer than gc_grace_seconds must not rejoin as-is, and, inside git, the reflog of the remote-tracking ref `refs/remotes/<remote>/tickets`, which records each fetch time. The plan neither considers this signal nor explains why the event-timestamp stand-in is better. It also never names the case where the stand-in gives a wrong answer that loses work.
scenarios: A clone keeps fetching (so it has converged recently), but one auto-push failed or was refused, leaving a single event with an old `ts`. It gets classified stale and the fresh work is discarded, which ADR §5 does not require.
A clone's clock is skewed backwards when it writes an event. That event's `ts` is earlier than the real write time, so the clone is wrongly classified stale and loses work.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the stale override resumable: collect the replay set and record a pending-replay marker before `reset --hard`, have the next reconverge finish any pending replay, and add a test that interrupts between the reset and the replay commit.
evidence: "Point `refs/rebar/stale-override/<utc-stamp>` at the old local HEAD ... then `reset --hard` to the pinned remote commit."
"A fresh clone re-adds its unpushed event files ... in ONE local commit on top of the remote"
sync.py:126-129: related history with no local-ahead → `reset --hard remote` (ff-adopt)
Testing lists no interruption or partial-failure case
findings.finding: The override is not atomic and cannot resume. It runs as backup ref → `reset --hard` → replay commit. If the process crashes, is killed, or the commit fails after the reset and before the replay commit lands, HEAD equals the remote tip. The next `_do_reconverge` then finds a merge-base and takes the related-history ff/reset path (`sync.py:126-129`), so the override never runs again. The fresh clone's unpushed events stay stranded in the backup ref, and any half-written replay files in the worktree get wiped by the next `reset --hard`.
scenarios: SIGKILL or a lock-timeout teardown between the reset and the replay commit on a fresh clone
The replay `git commit` fails (hook, disk full) after the reset has already moved HEAD
findings.suggested_fix: Build the replay set (file paths + bytes) before resetting. Do the reset plus replay as one atomic ref move: write the replay tree and commit with plumbing (`commit-tree` on top of the remote) and then `update-ref`/`reset --hard` straight to that commit. Alternatively, keep a 'pending replay' marker that names the backup ref, and have `_do_reconverge` check it first.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Either base staleness on an actual last-convergence signal, or classify each unpushed event individually (replay in-horizon events, drop only past-horizon ones), and add a test for a clone holding one old and one recent unpushed event.
evidence: "The clone is *stale* iff its oldest unpushed event's `ts` is older than `now − [reclaim].horizon_days` ... Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence."
"A stale clone replays nothing"
findings.finding: The staleness test is a proxy that can discard recent writes, beyond the loss ADR 0106 §5 accepts. The plan treats 'oldest unpushed event older than the horizon' as equivalent to 'last convergence predates the horizon', on the grounds that every write auto-pushes (I5). That breaks when fetch/reconverge keeps working but a push failed and was never retried. Such a clone converged recently, yet one old stuck event would mark it stale and throw away ALL its unpushed events, including those from the last few hours.
findings.location: Approach step 2 (Stale vs fresh); Approach step 4
scenarios: A push was rejected or failed long ago and was never retried, while background fetch and reconverge kept running and the user kept writing

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State and test the override's behaviour on a dirty tickets worktree: either refuse the override (keep DIVERGED) or snapshot uncommitted files into the backup commit before the reset.
evidence: "Point refs/rebar/stale-override/<utc-stamp> at the old local HEAD (local only, never pushed), then reset --hard"
findings.finding: `reset --hard` discards uncommitted or untracked state in the tickets worktree. The backup ref captures only the committed HEAD, so anything written but not yet committed when the override runs is destroyed unrecoverably. The plan does not say whether a dirty worktree blocks the override or is captured.
scenarios: An event file was written but its commit failed or was interrupted earlier; the override then wipes it.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the invariant 'reclamation records every removed event uuid in a surviving SNAPSHOT's source_event_uuids' (to be honoured by S2). Add a test where the remote dropped a retired file and a whole ticket dir without trace, and pin the expected behaviour.
evidence: "A local event is unpushed iff its uuid appears nowhere on the remote tip — not as a file under the ticket dir (any suffix), and not in any remote SNAPSHOT's data.source_event_uuids"
The test fixture 'rewrites the remote into a parentless baseline', but the plan does not say this baseline mirrors S2's actual reclamation output.
findings.finding: The no-resurrection rule depends on every reclaimed event leaving a uuid trace on the remote tip, either as a file with any suffix or in a SNAPSHOT's `source_event_uuids`. The plan never states this as a contract S2's reclamation must honour. If reclamation physically drops `.retired` files or purges whole ticket dirs without listing their uuids, those local events are classified 'unpushed'. A fresh clone would then replay them: the exact resurrection the horizon exists to prevent.
scenarios: S2 collapses a ticket and deletes its retired event files; a fresh clone holding one of those events replays it.
A ticket deleted or purged on the remote has local events that look unpushed.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the order of `store_epoch_problem` and the supersedes check in the reconverge path, and require that the stale/fresh tests drive the public reconverge entry point rather than stale_override directly.
evidence: "compat.store_epoch_problem (src/rebar/_store/compat.py:198) already refuses unions across differing epochs"
"in _do_reconverge's unrelated-history branch, call the override when the remote supersedes"
findings.finding: The plan does not say where the new branch sits relative to the existing epoch guard. `compat.store_epoch_problem` 'already refuses unions across differing epochs', and a superseding remote by definition has a differing epoch. If that check runs earlier in the sync/reconverge path than the unrelated-history branch, the override is unreachable. If it runs after, it may need an explicit exemption. Only the `_do_reconverge` unrelated-history branch is named.
findings.location: Approach para 1; Scope bullet for src/rebar/_store/sync.py
scenarios: The epoch refusal fires first in reconverge and the clone stays wedged despite the new code.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add ACs covering the `epoch_lineage` round-trip and fail-closed parse, `superseding_record` lineage append (including null), the no-unpushed reset, and a caplog assertion that the stale WARNING names the backup ref and the discarded count.

Approach step 4: "logs a WARNING naming the backup ref and the discarded event count" — no AC and no test.
Testing: "a clone with no unpushed events simply resets to the remote with nothing replayed" — no AC.
findings.finding: Several described deliverables have no covering acceptance criterion. These are: the `compat.py` changes (`epoch_lineage` parse failing closed, `remote_epoch_supersedes_local`, `superseding_record` appending the old epoch or null, the lineage-preserving `write_compat_record`); the no-unpushed-events reset; and the stale-clone WARNING naming the backup ref and discarded count. The first two appear only in Testing; the WARNING appears in neither the ACs nor Testing.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Extend the doc AC to cover the `epoch_lineage` schema, a recovery procedure from `refs/rebar/stale-override/*`, and backup-ref retention; add a cross-reference from ADR 0106 §5.

findings.finding: The new on-disk contract and the recovery path are under-documented. `epoch_lineage` (a new field in `.store-compat.json`) and the decision to use lineage as rewrite proof are recorded only in concurrency.md; ADR 0106 §5 is not updated to point at the mechanism. The doc AC also omits how an operator recovers discarded events from `refs/rebar/stale-override/*`, and whether or when those refs are pruned. That recovery path is the only rollback for the destructive override.
scenarios: An operator sees the WARNING and has no documented way to inspect or re-apply the discarded events.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a 'Failure-disposition contract' stating, for each override arm (backup ref, reset, replay commit, replay push), whether it is retryable/transient (the next background sync retries, and HEAD is left at the old tip or the backup is resumable) or fatal (surfaces DIVERGED or NEEDS_INVESTIGATION).
evidence: "in `_do_reconverge`'s unrelated-history branch, call the override when the remote supersedes; otherwise keep the existing refusal unchanged"
"which the normal push path then delivers" (no disposition is stated for a failed or rejected push of the replay commit)
findings.finding: The plan alters the unrelated-history failure path from a uniform DIVERGED refusal to an override that has several new failure arms, and it states no disposition for those arms. The unstated arms are: the backup-ref write fails, the reset fails, the replay commit fails, and the push of the replayed commit fails. The plan does not say whether the caller then sees DIVERGED, a retryable or transient error that the next background sync retries, or a fatal error. Only the malformed-lineage arm has a stated disposition (fails closed to DIVERGED).
scenarios: The reset succeeds but the replay commit hits a disk error. It is unclear whether the next sync retries, reports DIVERGED, or proceeds with events lost.
findings.suggested_fix: Retry policy: a failure in the backup-ref write, the reset or the replay commit leaves HEAD at the old tip and is transient; the next reconverge retries it. A failed push of the replay commit is handled as an ordinary transient push failure on the existing path.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In Approach step 4, specify that the fresh-replay commit uses `event_commit_git._git_add` + `_git_commit_paths` (pathspec-scoped, index-lock/transient retry, `_AUTOMAINT_OFF`) instead of new raw `git add`/`git commit` calls in stale_override.py.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] List every `sync.reconverge` caller (reads.py:265, doctor.py:226, fsck_repair.py:498, repo_snapshot.py:545, idle_sync) as a consumer that gains the forced override, and either accept that explicitly in the plan and concurrency.md or limit the override to chosen entry points.
evidence: src/rebar/_engine_support/reads.py:265 `_store_sync.reconverge(tracker_abs, lock_timeout=_RECONVERGE_LOCK_TIMEOUT)` on reads
src/rebar/_commands/doctor.py:226 and src/rebar/_commands/fsck_repair.py:498 call `sync.reconverge(tracker)`
src/rebar/_snapshot/repo_snapshot.py:545 calls `_reconverge(tracker)`
src/rebar/_store/sync.py:297 idle_sync → `_reconverge`
The plan names only `_do_reconverge` and documents the protocol under 'Inbound — background sync'
findings.finding: The new forced override, including its `reset --hard` that drops a stale clone's local work, will be reached through every `sync.reconverge` caller, not only background sync. Those callers are the throttled read path (`_engine_support/reads.py:265`), `rebar doctor` (doctor.py:226), `rebar store fsck-recover` (fsck_repair.py:498), the repo snapshot freshness path (repo_snapshot.py:545), and `idle_sync`. The plan does not list these consumers or say which of them may run the override. So an ordinary read command can now overwrite the local store.
scenarios: An operator runs `rebar show X` on a long-offline laptop. The read-path reconverge resets the store and moves the unpushed work to a backup ref, with only a WARNING logged on a read command.
An operator runs `rebar store fsck-recover` hoping to salvage local commits, and the override runs first.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make unpushed detection robust to re-compaction and retired GC: derive it from git history (files added by local commits not reachable from the pre-fetch remote-tracking tip), or close the SNAPSHOT chain transitively. Add a test where a re-compacted, GC'd ticket's old local events do not count as unpushed.
evidence: Plan: "A local event is *unpushed* iff its uuid appears nowhere on the remote tip — not as a file under the ticket dir (any suffix), and not in any remote SNAPSHOT's `data.source_event_uuids`"
compact_plan.py:131: 'A folded prior SNAPSHOT is NOT a source' — successor SNAPSHOTs do not carry earlier sources transitively
ADR 0106:27-28,44: retired-event GC is a 'secondary companion'
findings.finding: The unpushed-event detection assumes the remote tip still shows every uuid the remote knows about, and that is not guaranteed. compact_plan.source_uuids_of (compact_plan.py:128-137) leaves a folded prior SNAPSHOT out of the successor's source_event_uuids, and so also leaves out that SNAPSHOT's own sources. On re-compaction, events folded by the earlier SNAPSHOT are only visible on the remote as their `.retired` files and the retired SNAPSHOT file. ADR 0106 names 'a full `.retired` garbage-collection sweep' as a companion. Once that sweep removes those files from the tip, the remote has no trace of the events. A fully converged clone that still holds them locally will see them as 'unpushed'. Their ts is old, so the clone is classified STALE and its genuinely fresh unpushed work is discarded, along with a misleading WARNING.
scenarios: A ticket is compacted twice, retired GC runs, and then a publish-swap happens. A clone that converged yesterday and has one new unpushed comment is classified stale, and the comment is discarded.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that stale_override resolves the remote ref exactly once and uses that SHA for the supersedes check, the uuid/SNAPSHOT scan, the reset, and the replay parent.
evidence: Plan step 1: "appears nowhere on the remote tip"; step 3: "reset --hard to the pinned remote commit"
compat.py:226-230: 'Remote-tracking refs are updated by fetch outside the store write lock ... The caller must merge the returned commit, never resolve ``remote_ref`` again for that operation.'
findings.finding: Step 1 checks unpushed events against the 'remote tip', while steps 3 and 5 use a 'pinned remote commit' / `remote_commit`. Fetch runs outside the write lock (sync.py:261-276), and store_epoch_merge_target warns that the caller must never resolve the ref again. If the uuid scan, the supersedes check, and the reset resolve `<remote>/<branch>` separately, a concurrent fetch can swap the tip between them. The clone could then be classified against one commit and reset to another, and replay events that the newer tip has already folded.
findings.location: Approach step 1 vs steps 3/5 (remote_epoch_supersedes_local, reset target)
scenarios: A second concurrent sync fetches a newer tip between the uuid scan and the reset. Events folded on the newer tip get replayed, which resurrects them.
findings.suggested_fix: Resolve `<remote>/<branch>^{commit}` once at the top of the unrelated-history branch and pass that SHA as the only remote input to remote_epoch_supersedes_local and stale_override (all `git ls-tree`/`git show` reads use `<sha>:path`).

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that the override aborts (with local HEAD untouched) if creating the backup ref fails, make ref names collision-proof, and document plus test a restore procedure that pulls events out of the backup ref through the no-resurrection filter instead of resetting to it.
evidence: "Point `refs/rebar/stale-override/<utc-stamp>` at the old local HEAD (local only, never pushed), then `reset --hard`"
The docs AC covers 'backup ref, accepted loss' but no recovery procedure
No test for backup-ref creation failure or ref-name collision
findings.finding: The back-out path is underspecified. The plan does not require that a failure to create the backup ref (`update-ref`) aborts before `reset --hard`. It does not say how `<utc-stamp>` ref names avoid colliding, for example two overrides within the same timestamp resolution. It also gives no restore procedure: resetting to the backup ref would bring back the reclaimed history the horizon exists to prevent. No test checks the state after a recovery from the ref.
scenarios: `update-ref` fails (ref lock held, read-only refs dir) and the reset still runs
Two overrides in quick succession overwrite one backup ref
An operator restores with `git reset --hard refs/rebar/stale-override/...` and re-pushes pre-collapse history
findings.suggested_fix: Create the ref with `git update-ref <ref> <old-HEAD> ""` (the empty old-value makes creation fail if the ref already exists), add a uuid or nanosecond suffix to the name, and check the return code before resetting. Document recovery as a cherry-pick of event files filtered by the same unpushed-uuid rule.
